summary:
Delta State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies in the state with up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex unions, and no state-specific protective statute exists in Delta. Section 217 of the Criminal Code, applicable in Delta as a southern state, makes male gross indecency a felony carrying three years' imprisonment. The death penalty attached to Shari'a provisions applies only in the twelve northern states, none of which is Delta.

Enforcement in Delta has taken the form of mass raids on social venues. On 27 August 2023 police from Ekpan Division in Uvwie Local Government Area raided Teebolus Hotel on Refinery Road, Ekpan (Warri) at 9 pm, arresting 67 suspects at what police described as a same-sex wedding ceremony between Daniel Pius, 22, and Maxwel Ohwonohwo, 20. Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the raid followed a cross-dresser's confession that he belonged to a gay club travelling to a gay marriage ceremony; suspects fled on the officers' arrival and 67 were chased down and arrested. Police reported recovering drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses', kept the suspects and exhibits in custody, and continued efforts to arrest fleeing members for prosecution. One suspect alleged he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated. Coverage of the incident framed the arrests alongside drug allegations.

The same raid is recorded differently across sources: the UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note, citing the USSD 2023 human rights report, describes a 27 August 2023 Delta State raid on a 'white party' organised by the LGBTQI+ community detaining more than 200 individuals, with police alleging a same-sex wedding while some civil society representatives disputed that account. Wikipedia's Nigeria LGBT-rights overview records the Warri case as the 'Warri 67', of whom 67 were charged to court. Earlier, in June 2018, police in Asaba arrested more than 100 party-goers at a hotel on charges that they were gays and lesbians; by July 2018 the detainees were facing homosexuality-related charges in court.

A human rights lawyer based in Warri told the Home Office that 'kito' (predatory same-sex assault) victims under-report for fear of prosecution. State-level documentation for Delta is thin, which does not demonstrate safety for a trans visitor.
tangentialFactors:
Delta's enforcement pattern mirrors the national picture of mass arrests at social venues, with the Warri and Asaba raids among the largest documented outside Lagos. Incidents in Delta have been publicly framed together with drug allegations, which can compound charges and complicate any account of what the raid was actually about.

The discrepancy between the police and civil-society accounts of the August 2023 Warri raid, and between the 67 charged and the 200-plus detained figure reported by the USSD, indicates that arrest totals in Delta are contested and may be undercounted in any single source.
localsOnly:
Delta State residents have no state-specific protective statute and no documented state-level mechanism for complaining about police conduct in these raids; the Delta State Police Command itself is the source announcing the arrests and continued prosecution efforts.

Residents who are 'kito' assault victims in Delta under-report to police because reporting risks prosecution under the same national framework the assailants exploit, according to a Warri-based human rights lawyer quoted by the UK Home Office.

LGBTQ+ Delta residents facing the 2014 Act's penalties and Criminal Code Section 217 carry the same exposure as visitors, but additionally face the sustained raid pattern documented in Asaba (2018) and Warri (2023), with no state-level protective legislation to turn to.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any of the 67 Warri suspects were ultimately convicted, and the current status of the Asaba 2018 case, are not sourced in this inventory; the record stops at charges being filed.

The discrepancy between the 67 arrested/charged figure and the 200-plus detained figure for the same 27 August 2023 date is unresolved: the sources may describe the same raid with different counting, or two separate events.

Whether the Warri raid targeted a wedding or a party, and whether the detained individuals were attending an LGBTQI+ social event or a same-sex marriage ceremony, is disputed between police statements and civil society representatives and remains unresolved.

No Delta-specific data on hate-crime protection, trans-specific violence, document-marker rules, or access to gender-affirming care was identified in this inventory.
